questions.stem: A 68 year old man noticed that the left side of his face drooped and his speech was slurred while eating breakfast. His wife timed it at 40 minutes before it fully resolved. He has hypertension and smokes. When seen in the emergency department 3 hours later, neurological examination is normal. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and regular and BP 158/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden facial droop and dysarthria that fully resolve, with a normal examination afterwards, is a TIA.

steps.x: Sudden focal deficit that fully resolved within an hour, vascular risk factors.

elim: A persistent lower motor neurone facial weakness, not a 40 minute episode with dysarthria.
Causes positive symptoms such as jerking, not a sudden negative deficit.
Causes sweating and confusion; he has no diabetes.
His symptoms resolved completely.

steps.x: E: Transient ischaemic attack. Sudden focal deficit that fully resolves (within 24 hours) = TIA.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman developed sudden weakness of her right hand at 08:00. In the TIA clinic the following day at 11:00, she still has weakness of finger extension and a mild pronator drift on the right. She has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which feature means this episode cannot be classified as a transient ischaemic attack?
o: Hand weakness rather than speech disturbance
Symptoms persisting for more than 24 hours
questions.e: By definition a TIA fully resolves within 24 hours; persisting deficit means a completed stroke.

steps.x: Deficit still present 27 hours after onset.

elim: Age is a risk factor, not part of the definition.
TIAs can cause either.
A risk factor, not part of the definition.
TIAs are sudden in onset too.

steps.x: E: Symptoms persisting for more than 24 hours. Not resolved within 24 hours = stroke, not TIA.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has an episode of painless loss of vision in his right eye 'like a curtain coming down' that lasted 6 minutes and then fully cleared. He has hypercholesterolaemia and smokes. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and regular and BP 148/88 mmHg. Fundoscopy and visual acuity are now normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely source of the problem?
o: Atherosclerosis of the left internal carotid artery
Atherosclerosis of the right internal carotid artery
Giant cell arteritis of the temporal artery
questions.e: Amaurosis fugax is the classic TIA presentation: an embolus from atherosclerotic plaque in the ipsilateral internal carotid artery transiently occludes the ophthalmic or central retinal artery.

steps.x: Transient monocular curtain-like loss with vascular risk factors and sinus rhythm.

elim: The ophthalmic artery arises from the internal carotid on the same side as the affected eye.
His pulse is regular.
Causes headache, jaw claudication and often permanent loss in older patients; no such symptoms here.
Causes bilateral brief visual obscurations with headache and papilloedema.

steps.x: B: Atherosclerosis of the right internal carotid artery. Amaurosis fugax = embolus from the ipsilateral carotid.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman had sudden numbness of the right side of her face and right arm that lasted 15 minutes and resolved completely. There was no tingling that spread, no visual disturbance, no jerking and no headache afterwards. She has hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. Her capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L. Examination is normal and her BP is 154/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden negative sensory symptoms (numbness) that fully resolve in someone with vascular risk factors is a TIA; migraine aura and seizures cause spreading or positive symptoms.

steps.x: Sudden, negative, resolved, with risk factors and normal glucose.

elim: Causes positive symptoms (jerking, spreading tingling).
Her glucose is normal.
Aura symptoms spread gradually over minutes and are usually followed by headache.
Develops over days and lasts weeks.

steps.x: E: Transient ischaemic attack. TIA symptoms are sudden and negative (loss of function).

questions.stem: A 69 year old man could not see anything to his right with either eye for 20 minutes while reading. There were no flashing lights or zigzag lines and no headache. The episode fully resolved. He has atrial fibrillation and is not taking an anticoagulant. Visual fields and fundoscopy are now normal. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and irregular.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A transient homonymous hemianopia in both eyes is a PCA territory TIA affecting the occipital cortex behind the chiasm; atrial fibrillation is a classic embolic source.

clues: anything to his right with either eye
steps.x: Transient right homonymous field loss in AF.

elim: Affects one eye only; he lost the right visual field in both eyes.
Causes positive phenomena such as zigzag lines, usually with headache.
The deficit has fully resolved, so this is not an infarct.
Monocular, persistent and often with flashes and floaters.

steps.x: D: Posterior circulation transient ischaemic attack. Transient homonymous hemianopia = PCA territory TIA.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man had a 30 minute episode of left arm weakness yesterday that fully resolved. He has hypertension and smokes. He asks whether it matters as he now feels completely well. Examination is normal. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 162/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most important complication he is at risk of?
questions.e: A TIA is a warning sign of impending stroke; the risk of ischaemic stroke is highest in the days following, which is why assessment is urgent.

steps.x: Resolved TIA in a man who wants to ignore it.

elim: Not a recognised consequence of a TIA.
A TIA is ischaemic; this is not the main risk.
Related to falls and anticoagulation, not TIA.
A long-term consequence of repeated infarcts, not the main immediate risk.

steps.x: C: Ischaemic stroke. TIA = warning of ischaemic stroke, highest risk in the first days.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man had two 10 minute episodes of right arm weakness and dysphasia this week. He has smoked 40 pack years and has hypercholesterolaemia. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and regular. ECG shows sinus rhythm. Carotid duplex shows 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery with an irregular plaque.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his symptoms?
o: Embolism from a left carotid atherosclerotic plaque
Embolism from a right carotid atherosclerotic plaque
Haemorrhage into the left internal capsule
Vasospasm of the middle cerebral artery
questions.e: Carotid atherosclerosis is a major embolic source in TIA: plaque rupture or thrombus embolises distally to the ipsilateral hemisphere, causing contralateral symptoms.

clues: 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery
steps.x: Left hemisphere symptoms with a tight left carotid stenosis.

elim: ECG shows sinus rhythm.
Right carotid emboli affect the right hemisphere and cause left-sided symptoms.
A bleed would not fully resolve within 10 minutes.
Follows subarachnoid haemorrhage.

steps.x: B: Embolism from a left carotid atherosclerotic plaque. Carotid plaque embolises to the same-side hemisphere: contralateral limb symptoms.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin had 25 minutes of weakness of her left arm and leg that fully resolved. She was not sweaty or confused. Her capillary glucose at the time, measured by her husband, was 6.4 mmol/L. Examination in clinic is normal. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A sudden unilateral weakness that fully resolves with normal glucose is a TIA; checking capillary glucose excludes the important mimic, hypoglycaemia.

steps.x: Resolved focal weakness with hypoglycaemia excluded.

elim: Not suggested; she has vascular risk factors and a sudden resolved deficit.
Excluded by a normal glucose at the time, and metformin rarely causes it.
Symptoms resolved completely.
Follows a seizure, which did not happen.

steps.x: E: Transient ischaemic attack. Always exclude hypoglycaemia; then a resolved focal deficit = TIA.

questions.stem: A 75 year old woman has two episodes she describes as 'funny turns'. In the first she suddenly lost power in her right arm for 15 minutes but stayed fully conscious. In the second she felt lightheaded on standing and her vision went grey in both eyes before she fainted for a few seconds. Her BP is 146/80 mmHg sitting and 118/70 mmHg standing.
questions.q: Which feature most suggests that the first episode was a transient ischaemic attack?
o: Focal loss of function in one limb
Greying of vision in both eyes
questions.e: A TIA is caused by focal cerebral ischaemia, so it gives focal symptoms with preserved consciousness; global symptoms and loss of consciousness suggest syncope.

clues: lost power in her right arm
steps.x: Separate a focal episode from a global one.

elim: Global loss of consciousness is typical of syncope, not TIA.
A presyncopal symptom from global hypoperfusion.
Explains the second episode (orthostatic syncope).
Suggests orthostatic hypotension.

steps.x: B: Focal loss of function in one limb. TIA = focal symptoms; syncope = global.

questions.stem: An 81 year old man was talking to his daughter when his words suddenly came out muddled and he could not find the names of objects. His right hand felt weak. After 20 minutes he was back to normal. He did not lose consciousness or have any jerking. Examination now is normal. His pulse rate is 66 bpm and BP 164/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden dysphasia with unilateral weakness that completely resolves is a TIA in the left hemisphere.

clues: could not find the names of objects
steps.x: Sudden speech disturbance and arm weakness that resolved.

elim: Fluctuating global confusion over hours to days, not a 20 minute focal episode.
Not supported by a sudden, resolved vascular-pattern deficit in an older hypertensive man.
The deficit has fully resolved.
Follows a seizure, which did not happen.

steps.x: E: Transient ischaemic attack. Resolved dysphasia + weakness = TIA (left hemisphere).

questions.stem: A 63 year old man is seen in the TIA clinic 18 hours after a 20 minute episode of slurred speech and left hand weakness. He is anxious that 'something will show up'. He has hypertension. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and regular and BP 152/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on neurological examination?
questions.e: In a TIA, symptoms have fully resolved and the examination is usually normal by the time of assessment; the diagnosis is clinical, from the history, with urgent specialist review.

steps.x: Resolved episode, examined the next day.

elim: Would mean a persisting deficit.
A persisting sign means stroke, not TIA.
A persisting upper motor neurone sign suggests infarction.
Suggests carotid dissection or a brainstem lesion.

steps.x: D: No abnormality. TIA: examination normal by the time of assessment; diagnosis is from the history.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman had transient painless loss of vision in her left eye for 5 minutes, like a shade being drawn down. Vision is now normal. Her left carotid has a bruit. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and regular and BP 150/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which artery is most likely to have been transiently occluded?
questions.e: Amaurosis fugax reflects transient occlusion of the ophthalmic or central retinal artery, a branch of the ipsilateral internal carotid.

clues: like a shade being drawn down
steps.x: Transient left monocular loss with a left carotid bruit.

elim: Would cause right-sided weakness or dysphasia.
Would cause a right homonymous hemianopia in both eyes.
Involved in giant cell arteritis; it does not supply the retina.
Would affect the right eye.

steps.x: B: Left ophthalmic (central retinal) artery. Amaurosis fugax = transient ophthalmic/central retinal artery occlusion.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman had 20 minutes of right arm weakness that has resolved. She takes ramipril for hypertension and atorvastatin. She has never smoked. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and irregularly irregular, BP 142/84 mmHg. Examination is otherwise normal. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG in clinic
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves: atrial fibrillation.

questions.q: Which is the most important risk factor for this episode?
questions.e: Atrial fibrillation is a major risk factor for TIA and stroke, causing cardioembolism; it changes treatment to anticoagulation.

steps.x: Irregularly irregular pulse in a resolved focal episode.

elim: Not the key risk factor here.
A risk factor, but treated and less important than AF.
A risk factor, but treated, and the ECG shows a strong embolic source.
She has never smoked.

steps.x: A: Atrial fibrillation. AF is a key TIA risk factor and needs anticoagulation.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man suddenly could not lift his right foot while walking and dragged his right leg for 25 minutes. His arm, face and speech were unaffected. He then recovered completely. He has hypertension and peripheral arterial disease. Examination now is normal. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 166/92 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A sudden, unilateral, fully resolving focal deficit (here in the ACA territory) in a vascular patient is a TIA.

clues: dragged his right leg for 25 minutes
steps.x: Sudden resolved leg weakness in a vascular patient.

elim: Causes persistent foot drop, often after leg crossing or fibular injury.
Causes pain on walking, relieved by rest, not weakness.
Causes back and leg pain with persistent weakness.
Symptoms would persist.

steps.x: E: Transient ischaemic attack. Any sudden focal deficit that resolves fully = TIA.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with type 2 diabetes treated with insulin is found by his wife slurring his words with weakness of his left arm. When the paramedic arrives 10 minutes later the symptoms are improving. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 144/82 mmHg. He is clammy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: A bedside capillary glucose excludes hypoglycaemia, an important TIA and stroke mimic, especially in someone on insulin.

steps.x: On insulin, clammy, transient focal deficit.

elim: Part of later work-up.
Useful, but a reversible mimic must be excluded first.
Done in the TIA clinic, not first.
Not the first test; hypoglycaemia can be excluded in seconds.

steps.x: A: Capillary blood glucose. First test in any suspected TIA: capillary glucose.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman is seen in the TIA clinic after 30 minutes of left face and arm weakness that resolved. She mentions occasional palpitations. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and feels regular today and BP 146/84 mmHg. Examination is normal. MRI shows no infarct and carotid duplex shows less than 30% stenosis bilaterally.
questions.q: Which investigation is most likely to identify the cause?
questions.e: ECG for AF is part of TIA work-up; with palpitations and a regular pulse today, prolonged monitoring looks for paroxysmal AF, which would change treatment to anticoagulation.

steps.x: Palpitations, regular pulse now, carotids clear.

elim: Carotid imaging is already reassuring.
For seizures.
Not indicated.
Considered in younger patients with no cause; paroxysmal AF is more likely here.

steps.x: A: Ambulatory ECG monitoring. Look for (paroxysmal) AF with ECG monitoring after TIA.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man had a 15 minute episode of dysphasia 2 days ago. He is seen in the specialist TIA clinic, where the stroke physician wants to look for a small area of infarction and the vascular territory involved. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 148/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: NICE recommends MRI, with diffusion-weighted imaging preferred, in the specialist TIA clinic (ideally within 24 hours of referral) to show territory and any infarction.

clues: small area of infarction and the vascular territory
steps.x: Brain imaging in the TIA clinic.

elim: Less sensitive for small acute infarcts.
For seizures.
For subarachnoid haemorrhage or infection.
Shows fractures only.

steps.x: D: MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging. TIA clinic imaging = MRI with DWI.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with haemophilia A had 20 minutes of left arm weakness and slurred speech this morning, which has fully resolved. He takes no anticoagulants. His GP is considering referral to the TIA clinic. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Admit immediately for a non-contrast CT head
Give aspirin 300 mg and refer to the TIA clinic
Urgent carotid Doppler as an outpatient
questions.e: A patient with a bleeding disorder or on an anticoagulant with suspected TIA needs immediate admission for non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage.

clues: considering referral to the TIA clinic
steps.x: Suspected TIA in a patient with a bleeding disorder.

elim: Aspirin could worsen a bleed; a bleed must be excluded first.
Far too slow.
Antiplatelets are unsafe before haemorrhage is excluded.
Does not exclude haemorrhage.

steps.x: A: Admit immediately for a non-contrast CT head. Bleeding disorder or anticoagulant: admit for CT head first.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman had 10 minutes of right face and arm numbness that resolved 3 hours ago. Her GP finds a normal examination and asks a medical student how the diagnosis of TIA is made. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the basis of the diagnosis?
o: Clinical history with urgent specialist review
questions.e: TIA is a clinical diagnosis from the history, confirmed by urgent specialist review in the TIA clinic within 24 hours; investigations look for the cause.

clues: how the diagnosis of TIA is made
steps.x: Symptoms have gone and examination is normal.

elim: Identifies a cause, but a normal result does not exclude TIA.
Looks for AF but does not make the diagnosis.
TIA has no infarction by definition; a DWI lesion suggests minor stroke.
Not used to diagnose TIA.

steps.x: C: Clinical history with urgent specialist review. TIA is a clinical diagnosis plus urgent specialist review.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man is seen in the TIA clinic after an episode of left arm weakness that resolved. He is fit and independent and would be suitable for surgery if needed. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and regular and BP 156/90 mmHg. MRI is pending.
questions.q: Which investigation should be arranged urgently to guide further treatment?
questions.e: All TIA patients who would be candidates for carotid endarterectomy need urgent carotid imaging with duplex (Doppler) ultrasound.

steps.x: Anterior circulation TIA in a surgical candidate.

elim: For a patent foramen ovale in young patients.
For seizures.
Not indicated.
For young patients with no cause.

steps.x: A: Carotid duplex ultrasound. Carotid duplex for every TIA patient fit for endarterectomy.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman had a 20 minute episode of right hand weakness that fully resolved. She undergoes MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging in the TIA clinic the next day. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 144/82 mmHg. The radiologist confirms the diagnosis is consistent with a TIA.
questions.q: Which is the most likely MRI finding?
o: Bright area of restricted diffusion in the left MCA territory
Crescent-shaped collection over the left hemisphere
questions.e: In a TIA, ischaemia resolves before infarction occurs, so DWI shows no acute infarct; infarction would make it a stroke.

steps.x: TIA confirmed on imaging.

elim: Indicates infarction, which would mean a minor stroke.
A subdural haemorrhage.
Suggests multiple sclerosis.
An abscess or tumour.

steps.x: D: No area of restricted diffusion. TIA = no infarct on DWI; an infarct means stroke.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man had 15 minutes of left arm weakness that resolved. In the emergency department, capillary glucose is normal. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and irregularly irregular and BP 150/88 mmHg. Examination is otherwise normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: An irregularly irregular pulse after a TIA suggests atrial fibrillation; confirm with a 12-lead ECG as it changes management to anticoagulation.

steps.x: Glucose done; irregular pulse.

elim: Does not identify the arrhythmia.
For seizures.
Not indicated.
Not needed to identify the embolic source.

steps.x: A: 12-lead ECG. TIA work-up: ECG for AF.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman had 20 minutes of slurred speech and right arm weakness that resolved 2 hours ago. She is seen in the emergency department. Capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. She takes no anticoagulants and has no bleeding history or aspirin allergy. Examination is normal. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and regular and BP 152/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which medication should be given immediately?
o: Clopidogrel 75 mg and a proton pump inhibitor
questions.e: After a suspected TIA, give aspirin 300 mg immediately unless contraindicated, and arrange specialist review within 24 hours.

clues: no bleeding history or aspirin allergy
steps.x: Resolved TIA, no contraindication to aspirin.

elim: Thrombolysis is for an ongoing stroke; her symptoms have resolved.
Only if AF is the cause; she is in sinus rhythm.
Part of secondary prevention but not the immediate antithrombotic.
Used if aspirin is contraindicated.

steps.x: C: Aspirin 300 mg. Suspected TIA: aspirin 300 mg immediately.

questions.stem: A 65 year old man sees his GP the morning after a 15 minute episode of left face and arm weakness that has fully resolved. He is not anticoagulated. The GP gives aspirin 300 mg. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and regular and BP 148/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Within what time should he be seen by a stroke specialist?
questions.e: NICE: anyone with a suspected TIA should have aspirin 300 mg and be seen by a stroke specialist in the TIA clinic within 24 hours of symptom onset.

steps.x: Resolved TIA, aspirin given.

elim: Not required for a resolved TIA; that urgency applies to ongoing symptoms.
The old standard for low-risk TIA, now too slow.
Too slow.
Too slow; stroke risk is highest in the first days.

steps.x: C: Within 24 hours. TIA: specialist review within 24 hours.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman had a resolved episode of right-sided weakness 4 hours ago. Capillary glucose is normal. She had anaphylaxis to aspirin as a child and has a history of peptic ulcer disease. Her pulse rate is 68 bpm and regular and BP 146/84 mmHg. She is not anticoagulated.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate antiplatelet management?
o: Aspirin 300 mg with a proton pump inhibitor
Clopidogrel with a proton pump inhibitor
No antiplatelet until seen in clinic
questions.e: If aspirin is contraindicated, give clopidogrel monotherapy, with a PPI such as lansoprazole when there is GI bleeding risk.

steps.x: Aspirin contraindicated, GI risk.

elim: Contraindicated by her aspirin anaphylaxis.
Contains aspirin.
Leaves her unprotected in the highest-risk period.
Not indicated without a cardioembolic source.

steps.x: C: Clopidogrel with a proton pump inhibitor. Aspirin contraindicated: clopidogrel plus a PPI.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man is seen in the TIA clinic. MRI shows no infarct, carotid duplex shows 30% stenosis and ECG shows sinus rhythm. He has hypertension with a clinic BP of 162/96 mmHg and total cholesterol of 6.2 mmol/L. He has no contraindications to medication.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term secondary prevention?
o: Clopidogrel, atorvastatin 80 mg and blood pressure control
questions.e: Secondary prevention after TIA: clopidogrel (dual antiplatelet short term if high risk), high-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg and blood pressure control.

steps.x: Non-cardioembolic TIA, no surgical stenosis, high BP and cholesterol.

elim: Anticoagulation is for AF, which he does not have.
The high dose is short term; he also needs a statin and BP control.
Surgery is for 50 to 99% symptomatic stenosis.
Misses the high-intensity statin and BP control.

steps.x: E: Clopidogrel, atorvastatin 80 mg and blood pressure control. TIA secondary prevention: clopidogrel + atorvastatin 80 mg + BP control.

questions.stem: A 77 year old woman with newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation is seen in the TIA clinic after a resolved episode of dysphasia. MRI shows no infarct or haemorrhage. She has normal renal function and no bleeding history. She has been taking aspirin 300 mg since yesterday. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and irregular and BP 140/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term antithrombotic treatment?
questions.e: If AF is the cause, give anticoagulation (apixaban or rivaroxaban) instead of antiplatelet-only therapy, started once haemorrhage is excluded.

steps.x: TIA with AF and no bleed.

elim: Adding antiplatelets increases bleeding without extra benefit.
Inadequate for preventing cardioembolic stroke.
Antiplatelets are inferior to anticoagulation in AF.
Antiplatelet-only therapy is not enough for AF.

steps.x: A: Apixaban alone. AF TIA: anticoagulate instead of antiplatelets.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man had 20 minutes of weakness of his left arm 3 days ago. He is fit for surgery. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and regular and BP 150/84 mmHg. Carotid duplex shows 55% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery by NASCET criteria and 20% stenosis on the left.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his carotid disease?
o: Medical therapy only, as stenosis is below 70%
questions.e: Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50 to 99% (NASCET) on the side supplying the affected hemisphere needs urgent carotid endarterectomy.

clues: 55% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery
steps.x: Symptomatic right carotid at 55%.

elim: The left is not symptomatic or significant.
The symptomatic artery is the right one, supplying the right hemisphere.
Symptomatic stenosis of 50 to 99% qualifies.
Delays treatment when stroke risk is highest.

steps.x: E: Urgent right carotid endarterectomy. Symptomatic stenosis 50 to 99% (NASCET): urgent endarterectomy.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman had a resolved episode of right arm weakness and dysphasia. Carotid duplex and CT angiography show complete occlusion of the left internal carotid artery with no flow, and 15% stenosis on the right. She is fit for surgery. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and regular and BP 146/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Endarterectomy is for 50 to 99% symptomatic stenosis; it is not indicated if the artery is totally occluded, so she needs antiplatelet, statin and BP control.

clues: complete occlusion of the left internal carotid artery
steps.x: Symptomatic carotid fully occluded.

elim: The right is not significantly narrowed.
The right is only mildly narrowed and not symptomatic.
Endarterectomy is not indicated when the artery is totally occluded.
Her symptoms have resolved.

steps.x: A: Best medical therapy without endarterectomy. Total occlusion: no endarterectomy.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man has had four episodes of left arm weakness in the past 12 hours, each lasting 10 to 20 minutes and resolving fully. His GP sees him between episodes. He is not anticoagulated. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and regular and BP 164/92 mmHg. Examination is currently normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Aspirin 300 mg and routine neurology referral
Aspirin 300 mg and TIA clinic within 24 hours
questions.e: Crescendo TIA (repeated episodes) or ongoing symptoms need urgent emergency admission rather than a routine clinic referral.

steps.x: Repeated TIAs in hours: crescendo TIA.

elim: Too slow for crescendo TIA.
Recurrent episodes (crescendo TIA) need emergency admission, not clinic.
Too slow.
Unsafe.

steps.x: E: Urgent emergency admission to hospital. Crescendo TIA: emergency admission.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman had a resolved episode of left face and arm weakness 2 days ago. She has hypertension and smokes. Carotid duplex shows 40% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery by NASCET criteria and less than 30% on the left. She is fit for surgery. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and regular.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Best medical therapy and smoking cessation
questions.e: Endarterectomy is offered for symptomatic stenosis of 50 to 99% (NASCET); below 50% she needs antiplatelet, statin, BP control and smoking cessation.

clues: 40% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery
steps.x: Symptomatic stenosis below 50%.

elim: Neither side meets the threshold.
The left is not symptomatic or significant.
Symptomatic stenosis must be 50 to 99% for surgery.
Not indicated below 50%.

steps.x: A: Best medical therapy and smoking cessation. Below 50%: medical therapy, not surgery.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man had 15 minutes of right arm weakness this morning. He feels fine and wants to wait for his routine GP appointment next week. The doctor explains why he needs to be seen by a stroke specialist within 24 hours. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 156/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation for this urgency?
o: A TIA always becomes a stroke within 24 hours
The risk of stroke is highest in the first days after a TIA
The risk of stroke is highest one year after a TIA
questions.e: A TIA is a strong predictor of subsequent stroke, particularly in the days following, so urgent treatment and specialist review are prioritised.

steps.x: Why not wait a week?

elim: Many do not; the risk is raised, not certain.
His symptoms have resolved.
Risk is front-loaded, in the first days.
By definition it resolves without infarction.

steps.x: C: The risk of stroke is highest in the first days after a TIA. TIA stroke risk is highest in the first days.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has carotid endarterectomy for a symptomatic 80% left internal carotid stenosis. He asks how the operation will reduce his risk of a stroke. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: It bypasses the blocked middle cerebral artery
It dissolves clot in the brain
It improves cardiac output to the brain
It removes the atherosclerotic plaque that is the source of emboli
questions.e: Carotid endarterectomy removes atherosclerotic plaque from a significantly stenosed carotid artery, reducing embolic risk.

steps.x: Mechanism of benefit of endarterectomy.

elim: The lesion is in the carotid, not the MCA.
That is thrombolysis.
It does not affect the heart.
It does not affect heart rhythm.

steps.x: D: It removes the atherosclerotic plaque that is the source of emboli. Endarterectomy removes the embolic source.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has 25 minutes of left hand weakness that fully resolves. A medical student asks why her symptoms disappeared completely when her neighbour, who had similar symptoms, was left with permanent weakness after a stroke. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: Her symptoms were caused by a small haemorrhage that reabsorbed
The ischaemia was global rather than focal
The occlusion cleared before brain tissue infarcted
The weakness was caused by a peripheral nerve lesion
questions.e: In a TIA a thrombus or embolus transiently occludes a cerebral artery and the ischaemia resolves before infarction occurs; in a stroke infarction occurs.

steps.x: Compare TIA and stroke pathology.

elim: TIA is ischaemic, not haemorrhagic.
Infarcted brain does not recover.
TIA is focal ischaemia.
The pattern is central and vascular.

steps.x: D: The occlusion cleared before brain tissue infarcted. TIA = ischaemia without infarction.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man had 10 minutes of right arm and face weakness. Carotid duplex shows 75% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery and no significant stenosis on the right. A student asks why a left-sided narrowing caused right-sided symptoms. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and regular.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: Emboli from the left carotid cross to the right hemisphere
Emboli from the left carotid travel to the left hemisphere, which controls the right side
The left carotid supplies the right arm directly
The narrowing reduces blood flow to the right vertebral artery
The symptoms were caused by right carotid disease
questions.e: Carotid atherosclerosis is a major embolic source: plaque rupture or thrombus embolises distally into the ipsilateral hemisphere, whose motor pathways cross to control the contralateral body.

clues: 75% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery
steps.x: Left carotid, right-sided symptoms.

elim: Each carotid supplies its own hemisphere.
The arm is supplied by the subclavian artery.
The vertebral arteries arise from the subclavians.
The right carotid is not significantly narrowed.

steps.x: B: Emboli from the left carotid travel to the left hemisphere, which controls the right side. Carotid emboli go to the same-side hemisphere, causing opposite-side symptoms.

questions.stem: A 79 year old man had 20 minutes of left arm weakness. ECG shows atrial fibrillation and carotid duplex is normal. MRI shows no haemorrhage. He asks why he is being started on apixaban when his friend with a carotid-related TIA was given clopidogrel. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and irregular, BP 138/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation?
o: Clopidogrel is contraindicated in everyone over 75
Clots in AF are mainly platelet aggregates formed at high shear
Clots in AF form in slow-flowing blood in the left atrium and are fibrin-rich
Emboli in AF come from the carotid arteries
questions.e: In AF, stasis in the left atrium (appendage) forms fibrin-rich thrombus, so anticoagulation (apixaban or rivaroxaban) is used instead of antiplatelet-only therapy; platelet-rich arterial thrombus on plaque is treated with antiplatelets.

steps.x: Cardioembolic TIA, normal carotids.

elim: It does not affect plaque.
Age alone is not a contraindication.
That describes arterial (plaque) thrombus, which antiplatelets target.
His carotids are normal; AF emboli are cardiac.

steps.x: D: Clots in AF form in slow-flowing blood in the left atrium and are fibrin-rich. AF source = stasis, fibrin clot = anticoagulate.
